nameStory: The manatee mudflower gets its quirky name from its love of muddy, wet places where manatees might graze in its native Florida waters. The 'mudflower' part makes perfect sense when you see where it grows - along the soggy edges of lakes and streams where the soil stays constantly moist and muddy.
description: Manatee mudflower is a tiny aquatic plant that's actually quite rare to find in New England - in fact, it's been spotted here only once! This little Florida native is a creeping, mat-forming plant that hugs the ground and loves to keep its feet wet. It produces clusters of minuscule flowers and has small, simple leaves that help it blend into muddy shorelines.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that spread along wet, muddy ground, rarely rising more than a few inches high

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, simple leaves that feel smooth and slightly succulent to the touch, arranged oppositely along the stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Extremely small white or pale flowers clustered together - you'll need to look closely as they're easy to miss

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found right at water's edge on sandy or muddy substrates that stay consistently moist

habitat: In its extremely rare New England appearances, manatee mudflower would be found along the sandy or muddy margins of quiet lakes, ponds, or slow streams. It prefers areas where the soil stays constantly saturated but isn't deeply submerged, often in spots where other vegetation is sparse.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as temperatures warm, with the plant beginning to spread its creeping mats across muddy surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when tiny flowers appear in clusters and the plant forms its densest mats along water edges.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows as temperatures cool, though the plant may persist in milder conditions near warm water sources.
seasonality.winter: Likely dies back to roots or disappears entirely in New England's harsh winters, unlike in its native Florida range.

funFact: This little plant is so often misidentified in the aquarium trade that most people who think they're buying manatee mudflower are actually getting a completely different species - it's one of the most混up plants in aquascaping!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny creeping plants along water edges, but its preference for constantly muddy conditions and extremely small clustered flowers help distinguish it from most other shoreline plants.
contextualKnowledge: This plant highlights how global plant trade can sometimes move species far from their native ranges. While native to Florida, its popularity in aquariums means it occasionally appears in unexpected places, though it rarely survives New England winters outdoors.
compareHints: Since it's the only Micranthemum species recorded in New England, compare it to other tiny creeping plants in wet areas. Unlike many water-edge plants, manatee mudflower forms distinctly mat-like growth and has those characteristic tiny clustered flowers rather than single blooms or no flowers at all.
